q: You want to check which PermitRootLogin value the SSH server ACTUALLY uses, including files from sshd_config.d. Which command?
explain: sshd -T prints the effective configuration after all Include files. grep on the main file may show a value that a drop-in file has already overridden, and sshd -t only checks syntax.

q: A sudoers file contains: deploy ALL=(ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/bin/vim. Why is this dangerous?
options: You can spawn a shell from vim, and it runs as root
NOPASSWD is forbidden in modern distributions
It's not dangerous, vim only edits files
explain: vim (like less, find, awk, tar…) can spawn a shell (e.g. :!bash). Through sudo that shell gets root privileges. GTFOBins catalogs such programs.

q: The script /opt/backup.sh runs from root's cron and has permissions -rwxrwxrwx. What is the problem?
options: No problem as long as the owner is root
Any user can write commands that will run as root
Cron can't run scripts with 777 permissions
explain: The combination of 'run by root' and 'anyone can write' is a classic privilege escalation. The correct setting is 700 or 750, owned by root.

q: What does an 's' in place of the owner's x bit mean, e.g. -rwsr-xr-x root root /usr/bin/passwd?
options: The file is a symbolic link
SUID: the program runs with the rights of the file's owner (root)
Sticky bit: only the owner may delete the file
explain: The SUID bit runs the program with the rights of the file's owner. passwd needs it to modify /etc/shadow. The sticky bit shows up as 't' on directories (e.g. /tmp).

q: Which two SSH settings together shut down password login? (multiple answers)
explain: PasswordAuthentication closes classic password login, and KbdInteractiveAuthentication (formerly ChallengeResponseAuthentication) closes the PAM path through which a password can be requested interactively.

q: Which command finds files that any user can modify?
explain: -perm -0002 means 'the write bit for others is set'. -4000 looks for SUID, and -nouser for files without an owner.

q: Why is PermitRootLogin no better than allowing root login with a key?
options: Root keys don't work with ed25519
The attacker also has to know a username, and every admin action goes through sudo and records WHO did it
explain: Logging in as root erases accountability: the log only says 'root'. Personal accounts plus sudo give both an extra hurdle and a clear audit trail.

q: What does the auditd rule -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k identity do?
options: Records writes (w) and attribute changes (a) to /etc/shadow, with the key 'identity' for searching
explain: -w is a watch on a path, -p wa are the permissions being monitored (write, attribute change), -k is the key you later search with ausearch -k identity. auditd records, it does not block.

q: Which umask does CIS recommend so other users can't read new files?
explain: umask 027 yields files 640 and directories 750: the group can read, others see nothing. 022 (the default) leaves files readable by everyone.

q: Before restarting the SSH service on a remote server after a config change, what is the most important thing to do?
options: Run sshd -t and keep an existing session open until you've tested a new login
explain: sshd -t catches syntax errors, and the open session is your fallback if the new configuration still blocks logins.

q: How does CIS Benchmark Level 1 compare to Level 2?
options: Level 1 is for Windows, Level 2 for Linux
Level 1 is baseline settings with little risk of breaking applications; Level 2 is stricter, for higher-assurance environments
explain: Level 1 is a practical minimum for most systems. Level 2 adds measures that can reduce functionality and are applied where the risk is higher.

q: This file should enforce the SSH hardening from the lesson: key-only login and no direct root login. Click the lines that violate it.
snippet:
# /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-hardening.conf
Port 22
PermitRootLogin yes
PubkeyAuthentication yes
PasswordAuthentication yes
KbdInteractiveAuthentication no
MaxAuthTries 3
X11Forwarding no
LoginGraceTime 60
AllowGroups ssh-users
ClientAliveInterval 300
ClientAliveCountMax 2
explain: PermitRootLogin yes allows direct root login, so an attacker doesn't have to guess a username and there is no trace of who acted as root; use PermitRootLogin no. PasswordAuthentication yes keeps password login and brute force open; use PasswordAuthentication no. The other lines match the recommendations. After the change, check with sshd -t and sshd -T.
